what_its_for: Sulfasalazine is used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis (a bowel disease that causes inflammation and sores in the colon), and Crohn's disease. It helps reduce inflammation, pain, and swelling in your joints and digestive system.
how_to_take: Take sulfasalazine by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). Take it with food or right after a meal to help prevent an upset stomach. If you have the delayed-release tablets (EN-tabs), swallow them whole — do not crush, break, or chew them. Drink plenty of water throughout the day while taking this medicine. Space your doses evenly throughout the day as directed by your doctor.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take. A common adult dose is 2 to 4 grams per day, usually split into 3 to 4 doses. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and slowly increase it to help reduce side effects. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribes — do not take more or less without talking to them first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store sulfasalazine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids within 2 hours of sulfasalazine, as they may affect how well the medicine works. Limit sun exposure — this drug can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Wear sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid alcohol as it may increase the risk of stomach upset and liver problems. Do not take folic acid supplements without first talking to your doctor, as sulfasalazine can affect how your body absorbs folic acid. Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids every day.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin; yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); unusual bruising or bleeding; fever, sore throat, or signs of infection; severe headache, dizziness, or seizures; blood in your urine or very little urination (kidney problems); chest pain or shortness of breath; or signs of a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor if your symptoms are not improving after several weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: Sulfasalazine does not work right away. For bowel conditions like ulcerative colitis, you may start to feel better within a few weeks. For rheumatoid arthritis, it can take 1 to 3 months before you notice an improvement in your joint pain and swelling. Keep taking it as directed even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Sulfasalazine can affect folic acid levels, which is important during pregnancy. Your doctor may recommend folic acid supplements. Children: Sulfasalazine is sometimes used in children with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis or bowel disease, but the dose is based on the child's weight. It should not be used in children under 2 years of age. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, tell your doctor before taking this medicine, as your dose may need to be adjusted or this medicine may not be right for you. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to the side effects of this medication. Your doctor will monitor you closely.
